chunks: "There are two answers: an addressing limit and an electrical limit.
With 7-bit addressing there are 128 possible addresses, but 16 are reserved, so 112 devices is the theoretical maximum. 10-bit addressing extends that to roughly a thousand.
In practice the electrical limit comes first. The I2C spec caps the total bus capacitance at 400 picofarads for standard and fast mode.
Every device pin adds somewhere around 5 to 10 picofarads, and PCB trace and connectors add more, roughly 1 picofarads per centimetre.
So you can fit maybe 20 to 40 devices on a compact board, fewer on a long cable. The capacitance matters because the rise time is 0.
85 R pC b and has to stay under 300 nanoseconds at 400 kilohertz.
At 400 picofarads that forces the pull-up down below about 900 ohms, which starts to run into the sink-current limit.
And even before either limit, a lot of parts share the same default address, so collisions are usually the real constraint.
For that I use address-select pins, an I2C multiplexer to split the bus into branches, or a second I2C peripheral."
